extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical exposition on the metaphysics of the will, the role of suffering and death in moral conversion and salvation, and the epistemic limits of philosophy. Primarily an immanent (Kantian) account arguing that 'will' is the immediate datum and that suffering/asceticism effect the denial of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immanent scope of philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: My philosophy does not pretend to explain the existence of the world in its ultimate grounds: it rather sticks to the facts of external and internal experience as they are accessible to every one, and shows the true and deepest connection of them without really going beyond them to any extra-mundane things and their relations to the world. It is consequently immanent, in the Kantian sense of the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides philosophers to confine enquiry to phenomena accessible to experience; avoid transcendent speculation. Example: do not attempt to answer 'whence' or 'why' of the will beyond possible experience; these are 'transcendent' questions. Anti-pattern: building metaphysical systems that posit ultimately unknowable entities as explanatory primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence is unknowable
rubrics_metrics.description: All such questions ... are really transcendent, i.e., they cannot be thought by the forms and functions of our intellect, do not enter into these; it is therefore related to them as our sensibility is related to the possible properties of bodies for which we have no senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ultimate 'whence' and 'why' questions as outside philosophical cognition; label such moves as illegitimate overreach. Use the principle of sufficient reason only within the phenomenal sphere. Example: refrain from claiming knowledge about the being-in-itself of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge applies only to the phenomenal
rubrics_metrics.description: Where knowledge, and consequently idea, is, there is also only phenomenon, and we stand there already in the province of the phenomenal; nay, knowledge in general is known to us only as a phenomenon of brain... Knowledge in general is itself only a phenomenon, and therefore exists only in the world as the world exists only in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, require that they be framed in terms of phenomena (subject-object forms). Disqualify as cognitively baseless assertions that purport to describe the noumenal or the 'inner being' beyond appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The will is the primary datum and explanatory principle
rubrics_metrics.description: That their θεος is an x, an unknown quantity; the will, on the other hand, is of all possible things the one that is known to us most exactly, the only thing given immediately, and therefore exclusively fitted for the explanation of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'will' (the immediate inner datum) as the fundamental explanatory category when constructing metaphysical or ethical accounts. Reject explanations that posit unknown ultimate beings when the will suffices. Practical example: base an account of human motivation and world-objectification on the will rather than on speculative deity-concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics must be grounded in metaphysics of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: With me alone ethics has a sure foundation and is completely worked out in agreement with the sublime and profound religions, Brahmanism, Buddhism, and Christianity... The metaphysic of the beautiful also is first fully cleared up as a result of my fundamental truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for a satisfactory ethical theory: it should coherently follow from the metaphysics (theory of the will) and align with the soteriological strands of major religions rather than contradicting empirical human nature. Example: evaluate moral systems by their fit with the denegation/denial of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering and death as purifying/sanctifying means
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering is, in fact, the purifying process through which alone, in most cases, the man is sanctified, i.e., is led back from the path of error of the will to live... If, then, suffering itself has such a sanctifying power, this will belong in an even higher degree to death, which is more feared than any suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing spiritual or moral progress, regard suffering and the confrontation with death as legitimate and primary mechanisms for conversion/denial of the will. Examples given: criminal conversions on the gallows; the cross as symbol. Anti-pattern: optimistic doctrines that deny the educative role of suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy (aesthetic criterion) corrects the inborn error
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar effect of the tragic drama also ultimately depends upon the fact that it shakes that inborn error by vividly presenting in a great and striking example the vanity of human effort and the nothingness of this whole existence, and thus discloses the profound significance of life; hence it is recognised as the sublimest form of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the corrective power of tragic art as an evaluative standard for aesthetic works: great tragedy reveals life's vanity and helps turn the will away from mere pursuit of happiness. Anti-pattern: artworks that merely flatter the will-to-live or promise facile happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism as deliberate path to salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of the ascetics is the opposite of this. They make their life intentionally as poor, hard, and empty of pleasure as possible, because they have their true and ultimate welfare in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intentional renunciation, poverty and disciplined suffering as valid and effective practices for achieving denial of the will. In assessing religious or spiritual disciplines, give weight to whether they systematically reduce attachments and pleasures (examples: Trappists, mendicant orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Life is arranged to frustrate happiness and thereby purify the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Life rather presents itself as specially intended to be such that we shall not feel ourselves happy in it, for through its whole nature it bears the character of something for which we have no taste, which must be endured by us... Thus certainly everything in life is calculated to recall us from that original error, and to convince us that the end of our existence is not to be happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging doctrines about the aim of life, prefer those that recognize suffering and frustration as instrumental to ethical/spiritual development. Anti-pattern: philosophies or self-help ideologies that assume life is fundamentally arranged to secure happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective moral assessment requires foreknowledge of death
rubrics_metrics.description: The completed course of life upon which the dying man looks back has an effect upon the whole will... Just because a sudden death makes this retrospect impossible, the Church regards such a death as a misfortune, and prays that it should be averted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the moral/cathartic completion of a life by whether the agent had the opportunity for reflective retrospect (contemplation of life before death). Consider sudden death as preventing a full conversion/retrospective moral synthesis; use this when interpreting cases of late repentance or lack thereof.
